speaker: The Chairman
text: Head T, Ministry of National Development, Miss Cheryl Chan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When we look around a mature estate like those in Queenstown, Tiong Bahru and Bedok, you will notice that the exterior facades of the flats are well maintained, amenities abound within the community and signs of life around the neighourbood through the day.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To upkeep the estates, HDB has implemented many initiatives to renew and refresh each estate from time to time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Key programmes have so far served its designated purposes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But as time passes, an estate’s soul and vibrancy will go beyond the basic infrastructural projects and maintenance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the shift in demographics, new BTOs injected, fresh needs and immediate concerns resulting from the pandemic, changing lifestyles and business innovations, there is an increasing need to adapt and make our estates more liveable for now and the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While ground needs change and estates mature with age, the physical condition of estates is just but one aspect that needs to be looked at.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The vibrancy and people who live, work and play at these estates become central to the concepts that has to be refreshed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I wish to offer my suggestions on how to do this.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, creating co-working and study spaces in neighbourhood estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With COVID-19, the trend of work from home and home-based learning are on the rise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is likely to stay but not all households will have conducive environment that facilitates the activities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As such, some planning on designated areas in different estates will help provide the growing demand for future usage closer to home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We should consider this not solely from a commercial operating angle but bring local SMEs and platform providers to create the facility.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, this can benefit the vulnerable groups living in shared or rental flats who are unable to afford the space or technology gadgets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, provide communal spaces for people with disabilities (PWDs) or special needs to integrate amongst the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In 2020 COS, I raised the need for intentional efforts to do this.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With pervasiveness of digital technology, apps that provide information on venues and services friendly to PWDs can be made available.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I also recommended improving their daily assisted living within the public housing through the use of technology assisted devices to ease their burden on the long run.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Be it within the public flats or surroundings, familiarity and having the right aids in place are critical for them to live comfortably.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Third, augment talent and skilled labour force from the community for maintenance of estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As estates aged, it is common to have issues of spalling concrete, water seepage, leakages within the flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While HDB attempts to resolve such matters, there has been a lack of contractors from time to time to solve the issues.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The constraint of workers may persist in future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Given the demand for such maintenance, we should look at how to augment with skilled individuals equipped with skillsets to supervise works or certify them on contract jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Fourth, create more Wellness community areas with residents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are open spaces below or between the blocks of HDB flats, particularly at mature estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Besides the usual playground and fitness corners, we should consider working with NParks, residents and Town Councils to redevelop these pockets for green activities, community gathering points, exercise routes and link services around the area for all ages.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Think of each pocket as a mini-Botanic Garden which can be inter-connected through each division and finally linked to park connectors or the Green Belts under the urban planning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: More importantly, the social network and programmes are self-run by residents in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Retirees and volunteers can run regular social programmes to engage the community at this place, look out for other seniors who need care management, share meaningful time together on activities without tapping on resources from the agencies after the master planning and development is put in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These Wellness Community areas will keep residents active, healthy and bring vibrancy to vacant land areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Neighbourhood shops are useful amenities in any community and serve a diverse group of residents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, the growing presence of online purchases and declining variety of businesses in the neighbourhood, have put in question the relevance of these shops.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The last mile connection of essential services and products delivery can be co-located with these shops to leverage its convenience, provide community jobs and attract footfall that injects life to the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Residents frequently feedback on their worries that the concrete slabs may fall onto them, and the exposed rusting steel bars are also very unsightly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The lifts in those blocks are also very old and difficult to maintain.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: HDB keeps arranging for the spalling concrete to be repaired but they keep recurring and the spalling concrete pose a risk to the occupants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, when I see the design of the newer BTO flats, I feel envious and wonder whether some of the new features can be introduced to the older estates.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If there can be some upgrading, then may I ask whether the residents of the estate or the community leaders can be involved in the upgrading plans?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What else can we do to rejuvenate older flats so that they will be more pleasant, more airy and not deteriorate in terms of the living environment?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry replied that there are currently no plans to roll out such a programme as external wall seepage can be prevented through regular maintenance by the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, Sir, I would like to suggest HDB to conduct cost-benefit analysis on whether rolling out a national programme for facade improvement and repair works for ageing HDB blocks would be a favourable option for such extensive works.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In general, such an option is preferred due to economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, may I take my two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I have continued to receive requests from residents with no same-floor lift access, asking when their LUP will come.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It seems like only if residents write in to HDB to ask for the upgrading will they be told the real reason for no upgrading to-date, for example, whether it is for reason of cost or due to technical constraints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Notwithstanding my PQ, I would like to reiterate my request for HDB to provide an update to residents living in all such affected HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It is good to give some certainty to residents, tell all affected residents upfront the reason why HDB is not proceeding with LUP, whether it s because of cost issue for that block or because of some technical constraints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: HDB should engage affected residents directly on its decision, on possible alternative lift installation methods, and also what can HDB provide to improve accessibility without direct lift access.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Two years ago, I filed a cut with MND on the safe use of park connectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I said that, depending on locations, the park connectors can be busy places and well used by many people for recreational purposes, as well as for commuters getting to or from nearby MRT stations or bus stops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I highlighted my concern about safety of park connectors, particularly the uncertainty regarding the appropriate use of lanes provided on park connectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Two years on, there are a few changes in some PCN.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In the PCN near my home, there is a change to the lane markings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The narrow lane has a pictorial sign showing "no e-scooter".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The wider lane has a pictorial sign showing a bicycle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Occasionally, there is a sign on a post asking people to keep to their lanes with the pictorial showing two lanes side by side, one for cycling and one for walking.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, in other PCN, there are only pictorial indicators for cyclists and people on foot without any line drawn, or worse still, no separation, no indication at all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Like what I have said two years ago, many people still walk on both lanes and from both directions, and cyclists and PMD users are often left wading through the traffic on both lanes frequently unsafely, especially during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Many cyclists are still using the lane for walking and many people on foot who are using the wider lane often do not keep left, including many people walking their dogs or pushing a stroller, forcing each other to swerve around them, including forcing cyclists onto the narrow lane.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Two years on, I feel that not much has changed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If we want to mix them, they have to try much harder to ensure safe and orderly use by different users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Their return will only exacerbate the present situation with the ill-disciplined and poorly policed use of the PCN.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as the CEO of a Real Estate Investment Trust and my family has interests in real estate development.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: COVID-19 has accentuated the structural changes that have been occurring in the real estate market.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The uncertainty arising from this pandemic clashes with the prescriptive nature in our planning regime.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it provides clarity and certainty for developers and owners, it equally inhibits their creativity and results in laggard responses to market changes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the years, the planners have injected greater flexibility into a prescriptive and segmented blueprint approach to planning.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While zonings have provided the clarity much needed for driving the urban transformation during the early years, they may not be conducive in an era where innovation and flexibility are key.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: White zones, allowing market forces to decide on the eventual use out of a pre-approved list, have been successfully introduced.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As an example, in the context of retail.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The digital disruption in retail that started with the advent of e-commerce, has challenged the traditional concept of retailing.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The transactional activity found in brick and mortar malls, has been greatly reduced.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In response to this, many landlords have actively re-designated more space to prioritise experiential consumption, to play an enabling role to e-retailers, and also increased allocation of social space to be aligned to the current expectations of consumers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we have witnessed, there are inherent efficiencies when market is given some autonomy in allocating the best use for available space.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps we can adopt a more exclusionary approach to the land use definition rather than prescribing what is allowed?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In other words, could we create a zoning where planners could continue to uphold the transparency of the planning regime by describing what is not permissible in the zone, conferring the private market the flexibility to interpret and build based on market forces and preferences?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are living in a world where we are able to quite efficiently harness myriad views to add to our collective wisdom.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Why not use this approach in our city planning as well?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our planning regime could be further enhanced with greater public involvement in the process.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having many different voices not only make any final plans arising from this process more socially acceptable, the plurality of views should make them more resilient in the face of uncertainty and new challenges.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nonetheless, with diversity comes greater disparity of opinions, and possibly higher friction and delay.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How should we balance the trade-offs between the value of greater ownership and resilience and benefits of greater efficiency in planning and decision-making?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, there are growing signs that the shortage of BTO flats may become a serious problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want to know if that is enough.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the forecasted supply shortfall in each of the next five years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In light of the constraints due to COVID-19, how is MND going to cope with maintaining the delivery schedule when the deployment of foreign workers has been hampered?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the introduction of new building technologies, a new focus in Budget 2021, going to contribute significantly to solving the problem in the next one to two years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our reliance on cheap foreign labour has inhibited technological innovation in the past and we are doing catching up now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Along with increasing new supply, we should also look into how to increase the number of rental flats to satisfy demand temporarily.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One potential source of supply is to delay the demolition of the old HDB flats that have been the targets of the SERS or Selective En-bloc Re-development schemes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another avenue is for the Government to rent the vacant private units in the non-prime residential areas from private owners who are willing to rent out at a reasonable price, and then rent them out to the PPHS applicants.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Housing is and will always be a very critical issue on our small island but more than anything, we should not bite off more than we can chew by trying to house too large a population.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is equally important for the Government not to make short-sighted decisions in destroying more forests while we try to overcome the current housing shortage problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, the design of modern towns, such as Sengkang, the constituency I represent, tends to be denser, with commercial spaces and similar amenities located in specific clusters, often close to a transportation hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such design, undeniably makes sense from an urban planning perspective and can help minimise residential complaints pertaining to routine business operations, such as noise or trash.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The upshot, however, is that, compared to mature estates, modern towns often sacrificed more widely distributed nodes for gathering and social exchange since commercial spaces inevitably fulfil this function.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another common feature of modern towns is that multi-storey carparks (MSCPs), especially those that go into the sixth or seventh floors may inadvertently be under-utilised, especially at the uppermost levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This reflects not so much poor planning as much as the inherent difficult of adequately forecasting parking space demand at the point of construction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As our Government continues to plan its transition of our transportation towards a lower carbon future, demand for private transportation may fall even further, releasing even more spaces in our MSCPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is precedent in the conversion of segments of the MSCP for uses beyond the parking of vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most notably, many MSCPs now feature car wash space, typically with self-operated water jet and vaccum machines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: HDB also grants permits for car grooming and car sharing businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, special dispensation has historically also been granted to Town Councils for setting up office facilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For operations, such as central kitchens, the businesses may find themselves co-located closer to their customer bases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, there are potential costs that have to be considered when commercial activities are allowed to operate on the top decks of MSCPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These include the obvious noise disturbances or expanded electricity baseloads but these are surmountable challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, noise complaints could arise just as easily when residents choose to play football in the low use upper storeys of MSCPs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, many coffeeshops operate on the ground floor below MSCPs and generate comparable needs for electricity load and exhaust management.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, it is not new that Singapore's urban form has, in part, been shaped by a stage of economic development.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1960s when the manufacturer of labour intensive goods, such as textile, garments and simple electronics were produced by MNCs for sale into the world market, factories were built in industrial sites.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the earliest HDB flats were built in Jurong to house many of the workers who were employed in the nearby factories.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic, occurring at the stage of Singapore's economic development where indigenous innovation must drive productivity growth has the potential to also reshape our urban landscape.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a network effect in achieving overall productivity improvement when most employees are to work-from-home (WFH).

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Before COVID-19, the norm was for most employees to travel to the office and to work from there.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If most employees are already in the office, it is inconvenient to have a few employees join in meetings remotely.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, during the circuit breaker period with employees in non-essential services being required to work from home, many have found that work could actually be performed reasonably well.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Investments have already been made in equipment to support work-from-home.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: An idea is to design space use to support work-life balance for employees and to support an innovation-driven economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To be sure, working from home can lead to overwork.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is hard to stop answering work-related emails, for example.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, the flexibility afforded by WFH may allow, say, both husband and wife to work and fulfil the need to provide childcare and eldercare.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To work effectively from home, it helps to have an office within the house.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For those without this, having access to specially design office space akin to a business centre in the HDB block might rise job satisfaction and worker productivity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Future designs of HDB blocks may seek to cater to these needs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is too early to predict with any certainty the evolution of demand and supply conditions for office spaces in a post-COVID world.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, there is likely to be some scope for urban redesign.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: An argument made by some urban economists about why cities exist: because a lot of people in big countries concentrate together in a small geographical area.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And why workers in cities earn higher wages is that there are positive externalities when innovative people are in close proximity to each other.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: By exchanging ideas with each other, the average productivity level is raised.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore aims to nurture a steady flow of innovators in its next phase of growth, perhaps MND can be intentional in supporting greater interconnectivity and close proximity of innovators in its urban redesign, in a post-COVID world.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To sum up, COVID-19, with its attendant lockdowns, quite unexpectedly enabled the business sector and public sector to conduct a natural experiment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Can work be productively done when most employees are working from home?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is some evidence that work productivity does indeed improve when employees work from home.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Even post COVID-19, there is a real possibility that work-from-home arrangements in some form may become a permanent feature of working life.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There are then serious implications for urban design, both of the business district as well as the HDB heartlands.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We can undertake the task of urban design with technology to enable workers to achieve work-life balance and to support an innovation-driven economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, can I take my three cuts together?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Greenfield and brownfield development projects are both necessary as we continue to build up Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Yet, in selected situations, we have a choice on which way to go.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The recent discussions on greenfield development and the clearance of forest is a sign that Singaporeans are paying more attention to this issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Therefore, having a clear framework to think through this will do much to help our Government maintain public support in the necessity of large scale developments and persuade Singaporeans that our Government leaves no stones unturned in trying to achieve the right balance between sustainability and progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The changes brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic accelerates an increasing uncertain future in urban planning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Even with mass vaccination, there is a range of possibilities on what will be the future needs of our people and our industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: It will be helpful for our Government to tap on diverse views from the public and from the built sector on how we can finetune our land use policy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: In fact, I personally feel that there is ample room for the Government to partner and co-create with our built sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: URA's CBD incentive scheme and the strategy development incentive schemes are excellent ways to encourage the built sector to inject mixed-use development in the CBD.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Could we consider expanding this effort to areas beyond the CBD?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: An interesting international example is the Reinventor Paris competition in 2014 where Paris opens up sites to ideas from all over the world to respond to as existing challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, can MND share on how the Government can adapt our land use plans to respond to this changing trend?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: And can MND also share how we can consult and partner with our built sector or public to identify changing needs and new planning ideas?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Mr Chairman, vice-chair of the PAP Senior Group, senior housing is an issue that is very close to my heart and I spoke about this during the Private Member's Motion on senior policy in both 2019 and 2020.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: In particular, assisted living services for seniors are critical for seniors living in HDB estates to age in place with dignity and purpose.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I am heartened by the rapid progress made in this space.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I noted that MND, HDB and MOH launched an assisted living topology pilot, which is the Community Care Apartment in February.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Within my constituency, we have explored the benefits of assisted living services.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, I am certainly familiar not just of the complexity of such operations, but also the strong potential of such services to light up our seniors' lives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: So, on behalf of our seniors, I would like to MND and MOH for pushing forth with the Community Care Apartment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MND also share on the public response and the take-up rate and will there be a future launches?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The temporary development levy or TDL, is a tax payable when permission is granted for a temporary enhancement of the land value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The TDL can amount to tens of thousands of dollars payable by a small business every year and can form a significant portion of their business costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tenancy agreements seldom specifying who is responsible for paying the TDL and tenants are often in a weaker bargaining position vis-a-vis their landlords when the TDL is levied.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Often, the tenant is unaware of the TDL until they received the bill and would not have factored this into their business expenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can also be inequitable if the tenant bears the full TDL because the landlord also benefits from the enhancement of land value by being able to charge a higher rent to the tenant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, for some industries, URA grants temporary permission or TP for only one year at a time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can result in widely fluctuating TDL payable every year, making business planning difficult.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can URA provide businesses more certainty by providing them a choice of TP between three and five years to better align with typical commercial tenancy agreements?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will allow tenants to negotiate equitable rental contracts with their landlords and make other business plans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, some businesses have lamented to me that their TDL far exceeds business revenue, especially during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If businesses are unable to pay the TDL, they might have to close down, leading to losses to themselves, their landlords and their employees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government will also lose out on tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare that I work for a private real estate developer.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Our housing market comprises broadly two distinct sectors, public HDB and private.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I think the private sector can play a bigger role in innovating and scaling up new housing solutions to meet the needs of changing demographics, lifestyles and aspirations of our people.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Drivers for demand in the market is quite complex, with an interplay of many social and economic factors.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We may need to review some of the longstanding assumptions that continue to shape our policies.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: One recent trend that rapidly became the norm is work from home.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Its impact can be managed with a variety of new solutions.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: What is more complex to manage is our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just a quantitative issue, it is also about the quality of life of our citizens, both young and old.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It requires both hardware solutions, like age friendly designs, as well as software solutions like assisted living.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: And even if we found a suitable model, there is still the question of how to scale it up in a financially sustainable way so that we do not need to burden the state to continue to provide more subsidies.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Yet another trend is the reduction of household sizes.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Besides more singles and smaller families, I have observed families splintering up into separate households when they have the means to.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, I have seen examples of relatives or friends buying separately in the same apartment block to create a kind of interdependent household.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They are different from service apartments as they are meant for longer term stays.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I have observed overseas that they are attractive to young people, families, as well as retirees.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They are professionally managed, often with handymen service, housekeeping or community engagement programmes.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For retirees, they provide an option to monetise their homes and go for professionally managed rentals.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: HDB has been very proactive in coming up with new solutions.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In our highly regulated environment, the Government policies have a big impact in shaping the future of housing.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The form of public/private sector participation as well.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government will find it useful to review a number of areas to encourage active and responsible participation by the private sector.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: These include land supply, zoning and development policies, how we attract capital and manage liquidity, how to encourage adoption of technologies and how to create a healthy eco-system of innovative developers and service providers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, for our limited land area, Singapore's planning paradigm has been one of maximising the intensity of land use.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: COVID-19's economic impact may mean a need to re-evaluate our planning policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The Minister for National Development has likewise noted the same in an earlier statement, that while it remains to be seen if the shift seen in COVID-19 will persist in the new normal, as technology changes and advances, there is a need to take a good hard look at land use needs for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: For example, the circuit breaker period has also shown the viability of working from home, which reduces the need for traditional single use commercial buildings and areas.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Land use is governed largely by the URA Concept Plan and Master Plan, the latter of which is reviewed every five years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: However, beyond absolute land use designations and fixed plot ratios, such planning can arguably have more flexibility, considering the blurring of lines between different building use types, the prevalence of mixed use developments and higher frequency of building repurposing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I recognise that the CBD Incentive Scheme and the Strategic Development Incentive Scheme were introduced with the aim of encouraging the rejuvenation of the CBD and other strategic areas in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Is the Government re-evaluating the conditions of the scheme to adapt to the post COVID-19 landscape today?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And would the Government consider extending the rejuvenation schemes across the island to recognise and encourage greater creativity and flexibility in maximising the best use of our land and buildings?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, divorce proceedings are unfortunately more common than we would like them to be in Singapore, and the ownership of HDB flats is likely to come up as an issue in many of them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Individuals from the marriage without children are only allowed to retain the flat if they meet eligibility conditions such as being a Singapore Citizen, are at least 35 years old, and other prevailing conditions for retention of the flat under the Single Singapore Citizen Scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I recognise therefore for those with care and control of their children, they will be able to retain the flat subject to financial capabilities and other eligibility conditions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, while I am aware that our housing policies are pro-family and current HDB rules allow for some residents in the middle of a divorce to retain their HDB flat, others have not been able to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Individuals who are going through divorce proceedings are already going through a stressful period and mandating a sale of the flat adds on to the stress.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Individuals who are forced to sell off their flat may not be able to readily relocate and it may not be the most financially prudent option, adding on to the pressures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Further, some of them do have the wherewithal to continue servicing the housing loan by themselves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: While the HDB may be concerned about abuse, I believe couples do not enter the marriage with divorce in mind.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If divorce is already a source of significant stress, is there room to allow divorcees under 35 to retain their HDB flat, subject to meeting some prevailing eligibility conditions?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) currently enables couples or single parent families to rent from the Government while waiting for the completion of their BTO HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: With COVID-19 delays in HDB flat construction, there will inevitably be higher demands for HDB rental from families affected by the delays.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Beyond the PPHS, public rental scheme flats for the low income are also narrowly supplied, with demand outstripping supply despite a $1,500 household income per month cap for applicants.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Tightened controls for rental applications may lower the number of applicants, but not the real demand for the rental market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: There is a clear need for expanding a supply of rental public homes for those in need as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: On the broader landscape of change how is MND readying itself for a growing millennial preference to rent rather than own a house.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We have already seen the sharing economy take root in various areas of everyday life such as in transport, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This preference likely stems from both concerns on the affordability of home ownership and a preference for work mobility and flexibility.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Is MND considering expanding the supply of rental housing by the HDB to meet this growing demographic trend?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The reason is that some of these tenants may be elderly singles, who due to their age or behaviour, just cannot get along with another person in the same flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Others may be Singaporeans who had married a foreign spouse but cannot rent a flat due to the foreign nationality of their spouse.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: And then, there are also divorcees who had to sell the flat after the divorce but cannot rent a flat because they do not have custody care and control of the children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, when two singles who may be strangers to each other, and they are required to share a small space with each other, it does pose a huge stress point for both occupants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Their living environment would not be comfortable and they may have certain ingrained habits which make it difficult for them to adapt to living with each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: They have different standards of hygiene, different habits or medical conditions, and this may result in frequent quarrels.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: While it may be costly to allow a heavily subsidised flat to be rented to such singles, the government can show compassionate for singles who are truly in need.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I also urge the Government to consider having slightly bigger rental flats for families which may be larger.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: For example, if you have a couple with three or even four children, they would find it a squeeze to have to stay within a 2-room flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Basically, a 2-room flat would be a single bedroom with hall.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Many residents have to spend more time at home because of the work from home policy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This has created more tension within the neighbourhood and the HDB estate because the working adult who used to work in an air conditioned office may not be used to the home living environment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: There is more noise, there's possibly cigarette smoke from neighbours, and sometimes you may face unhygienic droppings from pigeons or cats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The silver lining, Sir, is that we get to spend more time with our families at home, and we are in closer proximity with our neighbours more than ever.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This is really a good opportunity to encourage residents to get to know our neighbours better, foster a sense of ownership for the shared living environment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: During the COVID-19 circuit breaker, some neighbours had set up a WhatsApp chat group so that they can order food together to enjoy economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The question is whether we can tap on this source neighbourly friendship to look out for one another.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: In that way, we can develop more mutual respect and understanding with our neighbours.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, permission to take two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: A resident of mine, Mr X, has a knee condition but kept delaying his surgery, in order to feed his four kids.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: His wife is unable to work due to a slipped disc for which she needs surgery.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Mr X cycles for hours every day as a Grab delivery rider to make ends meet, and I worry about what happens when his knees finally give way.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Another resident Mr Y in his 50s has to go for another surgery or one surgery after another.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The first to fix a workplace injury preventing him from working for two years, and then a stomach surgery for ulcer, and now he is being assessed for possible cancer.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: He cried to me, saying he feels so defeated because he cannot even afford to buy small snacks or treats for his grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: He feels that he has failed as a father and grandfather.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Although some of these residents already pay very low rent each month, thanks to the subsidies from HDB, the fear that they may lose having shelter over their heads is a real one and a real stress point.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Even $100 rent a month is a stress point for someone in Mr X and Mr Y's circumstances, and there are many of them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Even though HDB does provide additional subsidies when appeal letters are sent, the stress of having to go see a Member of Parliament, and uncertainty about outcomes is still a stressful process.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: A blanket waiver of rent for at least six months will give much needed reprieve to these families who live on the brink.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Land scarcity in Singapore is a fact of life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Amidst increased public pressure and attention on inequality, we need to provide better public rental housing in order to rehabilitate low-income families more effectively.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: How can we do so without incurring larger costs?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: On one hand, we have large families in small rental flats, struggling with overcrowding.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Single mothers and fathers are struggling to find care so they can go out to work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: On the other hand, we have isolated elderly in HDB flats, suffering loneliness, with rising risk of elderly suicide.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We can kill two birds with one stone, by putting isolated elderly and single parent families together to optimise resources for better social outcomes.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The cost savings from building new rental flats can be used instead as rent paid out to financially challenged and isolated elderly flat-owners, if they are willing to open up their homes to single parents and their children.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Such a programme would provide a larger housing supply without incurring more building costs, improve retirement adequacy for the poor seniors, reduce their social isolation as well as provide informal care and support for the children and youth of single parents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: (In Mandarin):   In Singapore, we have two groups of people who face different difficulties.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: On one hand, many large families live in a small rental flat and do not have enough space.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Single parents often do not have anyone to take care of their children when they want to work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: On the other hand, many isolated elderly live alone in HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Data shows that the risk of them committing suicide is higher.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Hence, I would like to propose this scheme whereby we put single parent families with isolated elderly together, killing 2 birds with 1 stone and solving the problems mentioned above.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Under this scheme, if the elderly are willing to let single parent families to move into their home, the authorities can convert the cost of building new flats into a sort of rental income for the elderly, and help reduce their financial burden.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: This will increase the supply of newer and larger rental flats and save construction cost.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: More importantly, the elderly will have company and children from single parent families will not become “latch-key kid”.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Implementation is bound to be challenging, as personality dynamics will play a big part in the success of such a programme.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: It is key that the matching of elderly to families is done socially and not purely administratively.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: I believe by having close collaboration amongst the ComLink agencies on the ground on such an initiative, we can see much improved social outcomes, with less costs, to optimise the care and well-being of our people.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, can I take my two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Can MND and HDB do more to address this issue?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We have seen cases from time to time of flat mates not having an easy time living together in the same flat.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: While they are thankful for being provided a roof over their heads, and at a level of affordability which is in line with their income, they are under a lot of stress to get used to living with someone who may be very different from their own personalities and backgrounds and who may not share the same habits and lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We have to be mindful that these are two strangers who have to stay together.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I hope the Ministry can do more to increase the level of comfort for them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Has HDB done any research or survey to find out what are the common issues raised and whether it had been able to resolve them?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: If not, would the Ministry consider doing so and keeping the records for future reference to inform officers assisting these tenants?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The task force should be empowered to mediate and make recommendations such as early termination of the Tenancy Agreement and matching or replacement of tenant and so on.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: They may be families with more children or have elderly parents and parents-in-law.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Due to personal circumstances, they are unable to live apart and it is not always possible to find them separate rental flats in the same block to house them all.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Hence, overcrowding becomes a big problem for such families, leading to tensions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Due to a lack of space, some members of these families might be staying out of the assigned flat due to the cramped or hostile atmosphere in the home.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is not safe for them, to be sleeping rough outside.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Their health and ability to study or work productively are also affected.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: For youths who loiter outside of home more often, this may lead to higher chances of them becoming wayward and delinquent, and expose them to crimes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of the work-from-home movement.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: With the current trend of working and learning from home, the need for more space at home for each member of the family has become more pronounced.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is no different for these families living in the rental HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Can the Ministry provide more information on how these needs have been met in the past and how can we provide better living environment for rental flat residents?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is especially so for families with school-going children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the lower income singles are in need of rental housing due to various circumstances and many are seniors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: HDB does help under the Joint Singles Scheme (JSS), which requires single tenants to rent a flat together with a flat mate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As they are single, many are unable to find a flat mate and are in the end housed with a stranger.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure many Members in this House would have handled MPS cases of flat mates not getting along.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand HDB’s concerns that there may not be an ample supply of rental flats to cater for every single to rent a flat alone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I understand MND does allow a person to rent a flat alone on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spent more than a quarter of my life speaking up about our policy of not allowing the keeping of cats in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I last spoke up about this last year, providing various solutions to the concerns MND has.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can change our policy to reflect what we already accept in reality – that HDB residents are allowed to keep cats, which can be removed if they are found to cause disamenities in the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is an issue that affects thousands who currently live in HDB flats and keep cats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sallie wrote to me recently and said, "Thank you for raising this issue again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is one of the reasons why I can’t come back to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two cats here in Bangkok and I have no place to keep them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can only afford to buy a HDB flat if I go home as I can’t possibly afford private properties." I hope this year and at this COS, we will finally have the good news that we will allow the keeping of cats in HDB flats with specific conditions that will address any issues of disamenities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I should add that Speaker supports this change in policy as well.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, the Minister for National Development has answered questions in this House on Community Care Apartments which is an assisted living typology pilot that is not just about housing but also the integration of care and social services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Ministry to share more details about its plans for future launches to keep up with market demand and, at the same time, because this is about care and social services as well, what are the Ministry's plans to ensure quality and sustainable development of services?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Also, bearing in mind that the services can cost quite a significant amount, how would the Ministry ensure that applicants who need these services, applicants for whom the assisted living typologies clearly designed for but may, nonetheless, have difficulties affording such services, how would the Ministry ensure that such applicants would not be excluded from the scheme simply because of financial means?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the ethnic integration (EIP) policy remains an important policy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It prevents the formation of ethnic enclaves and encourages Singaporeans of different races to mingle in the same community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It ensures that there is adequate minority representation of the population within the neighbourhood estate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But there are unexpected or unintended economic consequences from the EIP for the last few minorities in the block.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Amidst the pandemic, some Singaporeans who faced financial difficulties are seeking to monetise their flats and downgrade to a smaller one.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For a pocket of minority Singaporeans, this is particularly challenging as they have fewer to no prospective buyers to sell their flats to.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They may have to sell their flats at a much lower than market rate to make it more appealing to same ethnicity buyers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This price may barely cover what they have to pay for their new purchase which greatly impacts on their financial plans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have been approached by a number of my Malay, Indian and Eurasian elderly and middle-aged residents want to downgrade and sell their flat as they are in part affected by the COVID-related crisis or need extra funds for an emergency or healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It could also encourage them to sell their flats at a lower price to buyers of the same group.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, housing is an essential part of our lives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My flat is more than just an address.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During the 2019 National Day Rally, Prime Minister announced that prime land in Singapore Greater Southern Waterfront will be slated for urban development.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More public housing projects are also slated to be launched in city centre locations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, flats situated on prime land suggest a higher cost than most current BTO flats.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very grateful that we are piloting new models.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is critical and I am also glad that we are caring for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister whether there are studies or information on the potential impact of the new housing models on the values of existing flats around them and how can the Ministry ensure that new models of flats will not adversely affect existing home owners in the same area.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we stay in our homes, we do not just stay alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each block or street, houses the community and COVID-19 has shifted our lifestyles and many of us are spending more time at home and in our neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, COVID-19 has also brought about many positive stories and examples of neighbourliness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, sanitisers in lives or people who volunteered to buy food for those who may not have been as mobile.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is MSO leveraging this opportunity to nudge or grow community ownership of common spaces in good neighbourliness, and where neighbour relationships have broken down, how can agencies better work together to intervene and help resolve neighbour disputes in both public and private estates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, I am glad to hear that the Municipal Services Office (MSO) improves service delivery by leveraging on technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The AI-powered chatbot and OneService app appear to share some overlapping features.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the Chatbot introduction, what are plans for the OneService app to keep it relevant?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What functions are the Chatbot able to fulfill, which the OneService app cannot, and vice versa?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned about the chatbot's ability to accurately predict the case category and owner, based on the feedback.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What will happen if the chatbot is unable to make the correct prediction?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does it only accept feedback on municipal issues?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents may not be able to distinguish between municipal and non-municipal issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can residents be assured that their feedback will be adequately handled with no compromise to service quality, even if there is a mistake in the category?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, in Tampines North, I have been quite involved in the block repainting projects done by the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I feel that it is important that our blocks look good and residents live in a neighbourhood that they can identify with and have a sense of belonging.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Therefore, I have been working closely with the contractor to design colour schemes.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Some of them have become popular spots for Instagram postings.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There are many other estate improvement projects like Neighbourhood Renewal Programme and the Home Improvement Programme which require, and rightfully so, residents' support through a voting process.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Voting is typically done manually, requiring physical forms or manual voting.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This is especially so during the current pandemic when we need to minimise gatherings of people and physical interactions.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Such a feature could also be useful in gathering inputs from the community on local issues.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: For example, sometimes, we have residents complaining of people gathering at the void deck seating area during wee hours causing a noise nuisance, and requests to remove the seating.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, there could also be responsible users at other times of the day, for instance neighbours having a chit chat at the void deck or elderly taking a rest on the way home from the market.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We typically ask grassroots leaders who live there for their observations, but these tend to be anecdotal and may not be very data driven.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: A digital survey could reach a potentially different and bigger segment of the population to supplement the information for a better considered decision.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, during circuit breaker last year, many services came to a halt.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In a few months, trees and grass areas were overgrown, drains and common area maintenance were affected around the island.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While some people enjoyed the nature and welcome the sights of wild flora and fauna around the neighbourhood, there were others who were concerned about safety of overgrown tree crowns or affected due to allergy and sensitive health condition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I know that essential services had continued to be provided in as many areas as possible, but we had to face the reality that some services were unable to be carried out for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Since the introduction of OneService app, I have received positive feedback from residents about the app.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am also a user of OneService app and agree with this view.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, there are other feedback that closing the loop on matters can still be further improved.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Sometime, the approach used and resolution of the matter does not effectively address the fundamental problem or had not met the expected outcome of the complainant.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: MSO announced last year a series of technological improvements such as improving accessibility to services through OneService Lite and AI-powered chatbot.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am certainly supportive of using technology to enhance efficacy of processes and deliver more impactful results.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Over time, we need to evolve the OneService app beyond a reporting tool.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: During the re-opening of Phase Two, we have seen that the app being used by public to notify the agencies on cases of violation for not wearing masks and not complying to safe social distancing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This may have helped the management of safe distancing and accelerated the habit of public complying to new measures.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But, it may also have inevitably created the effect of some divisiveness in the community and not promote a positive sense of active citizenry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With an aging population, there is possibly an increase of seniors living without extended family support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One, for individuals with handy skills, they can help families do simple jobs of plumbing, changing fixtures, and so on, and earn some side income.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Two, volunteers nearby schools and community partner organisations can take this as value in action community project, to give back to those who are in need, such as assisting in grocery shopping and also help with the cleaning of their homes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we encourage more to join us on the sustainability journey, I am sure those who do not actively participate today, may want to know more or where they can begin.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The app can provide information for those interested to do community gardening, corridor gardening or urban farming; an opportunity to learn from others with green fingers, exchange notes and other green initiatives to be more successful gardeners.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Or the community can exchange secondhand items to reduce usage of new purchases and help some families save on expenses if they have spare resources available.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This way, we can become more environmentally conscious with more rallying each other to learn, exchange and reduce wastage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: High-rise littering, cat feeding, noise disturbances and smoking at unauthorised areas are long-standing issues that we have been tackling.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There is no silver bullet on how to resolve these.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But through availability of data uncovering the root cause and with the help of artificial intelligence, it may minimise the issue if we leverage technology, establish community groups and link them to outreach the offenders or the trigger points, so that they can work on education, encouragement of behavioural change together with various agencies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We may, in the course of action, meet vulnerable individuals and families who need social or mental healthcare that the community can provide to make a difference.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This goes beyond a carrot and stick approach in managing sticky issues.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe we should be open and pilot initiatives to check should this approach help reduce neighbourly disputes, while creating active participation from the complainants and others in the community to tackle the problems and find solutions together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The sector's direction is spelled out under the Construction Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Previously the Government has driven industry transmission in three key areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: One, design for manufacturability and assembly; two, integrated digital delivery; and three, green buildings.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Moving forward, what are the Government plans to encourage industry transmission in these three areas and are there any other areas of transmission that MND is looking for?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, there is a need to remake our city to prepare for climate change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: On this note, I would like to share some feedback on the Green Mark scheme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: On the good side, the influence of a Green Mark goes beyond our shores and increasingly it is the go-to standards that the private sector in nearby countries adopt.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: One common feedback is that we need to ensure that the Green Mark Standard is able to capture the big picture of sustainability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: For example, how do you build a building to maximise external air flow which will fundamentally drive down the cooling of the entire building.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: This is in comparison, making sure that the Green Mark Standard become more than just a checkboard place off, achieving high quality green standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, can MND share on what more can be done to improve energy and resource efficiency in the built environment sector?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: While necessary it is also adding in a new layer of complexity at the time when the built sector was at the crossroads, as per what I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The built sector has to juggle foreign and local manpower shortages, industry transformation, changing demand and industry downturn.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: So, while the many in the built sector whom I spoke to welcome the challenge, it is also important that we strike the right balance by consulting as many stakeholders in the built sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I also want to voice a word of caution as a Member of Parliament, passionate about sustainability, having green standards out is very good.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: But we must live sufficient room for added inputs to factor in the rapidly changing Singapore built industry landscape, as well as the post-COVID-19 need, so the new Green Building Masterplan can remain as relevant as possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, can I take my three cuts together?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Chairman, the built environment sector has been hit hard by COVID.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The Government has also committed to providing relief for some of the non-manpower costs that construction firms in public sector projects will incur due to the prolongation of projects and there has been legislation such as a universal extension of time to help all contracting parties bear fair share of the impact of project prolongation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And yet the sector continues to face an uncertain outlook this year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: In this light, how will the Government continue to support firms in the sector to recover in the near term?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: At the same time, COVID-19 has shown we must transform the built environment industry to improve productivity and, importantly, reduce reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Under the construction industry transformation map (ITM), the Government has identified two key areas.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: One, design for manufacturing and assembly, or DFMA; and, two, integrated digital delivery, or IDD.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I also understand that amongst construction tenders to be called in the next two years, up to 85 of these projects, both public and private, will require DFMA technologies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: For IDD, I understand that there are over 35 public and private sector projects piloting this, such as the Health Sciences Authority Building and Rochester Commons at 19 Nassim by private developers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Can the Ministry share further updates on the progress of both DFMA and IDD within the construction ITM framework?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And moving forward, what are the Government's plans to further drive industry transformation in these areas?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And more specifically, what would this mean for Singaporeans in terms of the number and type of job opportunities?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Mr Chairman, the built environment sector is made up of many interconnected stakeholders along the value chain, including developers, builders, consultants, contractors, facilities managers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Rather than a single firm or segment of the value chain transforming on its own, Deputy Prime Minister has announced the Growth and Transformation scheme for the entire built environment sector.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Can the Ministry share further details and, again, what would it mean ultimately for job opportunities for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Buildings account for over 20% of Singapore's carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Last December, Keppel Bay Tower became the first commercial building in Singapore to be certified Green Mark Platinum Zero Energy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Besides a low energy use index of less than 115 kilowatt hour per square metre per year, the building has all of its energy supplied through renewable sources, both on and offsite.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: However, as Minister Desmond Lee said earlier today, we need to do more to ensure that both our existing and future buildings in Singapore are designed to conserve energy and water and minimise materials wastage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Minister also shared about the "80: 80: 80" by 2030 targets under the next edition of the Singapore Green Building masterplan.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And as the Member Mr Henry Kwek said just now, the Government has also announced at COS last year that various stakeholders will be invited to co-create this next edition of the masterplan.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: In this regard, can the Ministry provide an update on its progress and what are the plans going forward?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, echoing the views of Members Mr Kwek and Mr Xie, the built environment sector took a severe hit as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Understandably, cashflow becomes a major problem as project milestone payments are delayed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In view of this tight situation, how can MND and BCA help the construction industry tide over this difficult period?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Looking ahead, the construction industry will have to accelerate industry transformation, to shift from heavy manpower-intensive processes and leverage technologies that enable higher productivity and effectiveness, for example, using drones for land surveillance and progress updates, robotics and autonomous platforms to assist workers in the heavy lifting tasks in construction sites.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Having said that, many of such enablers would require heavy initial investment in equipment and software and the retraining of existing staff.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can the built environment sector be further incentivised to adopt the latest technology solutions in construction, either to reduce the dependence on foreign workers or improve productivity in construction?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to ask about property prices in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Property prices have continued to rise, defying the typical downward trend in a recession.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, this past year, we have all had to wrestle with the challenges thrown at us by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But through close cooperation between the Government, industry and community partners, we have made good progress.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We provided significant support to firms in the Built Environment sector through one of its darkest moments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We worked hard to get our BTO projects back on track and assisted many buyers affected by inevitable construction delays.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For homeowners and public rental tenants who faced financial challenges, we helped them with their mortgage and rent payments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To assist businesses renting commercial or industrial properties, we put in place various cost-sharing arrangements and relief measures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But we are not out of the woods yet and must remain vigilant.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, we must keep our eye on the future, learn the lessons from this pandemic and come out stronger from this experience.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our work to build an ever more resilient, inclusive and sustainable Singapore must continue.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: One major enterprise is the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For these efforts to bear fruit, we need all Singaporeans to be actively involved.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that is why, over the past few months, MND agencies conversed with Singaporeans through nine Emerging Stronger Conversations about our city, our home and our environment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have heard many thoughtful suggestions and thank everyone who participated for their enthusiasm and passion.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And we will continue to reach out, in dialogue and partnership, to work with Singaporeans to realise their vision for our city and turn their ideas into action.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
